query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A single intervention that can simultaneously enhance low‐temperature activity, poisoning resistance, and long‐term durability in a near‐equiatomic, multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst is to deposit an ultrathin, conformal porous high‐entropy oxide (HEO) overlayer on the catalyst. This HEO overcoat is expected to stabilize the active metal nanoparticles (even minimal Pt or other PGMs) against sintering, suppress deleterious adsorption of poisons (H2O, NO), and enable partial self‐regeneration under thermal cycling.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst with low platinum-group-metal content that, while active, suffers from degradation by poisoning and sintering under transient, low-temperature, and harsh exhaust conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply an ultrathin, nanoporous high‐entropy oxide overlayer via techniques such as atomic layer deposition or electrospinning templated coating to uniformly encapsulate or support the catalyst.
generation.conditions: The modified catalyst should be tested under realistic automotive exhaust conditions featuring transient low temperatures (below 150 °C during cold start), exposure to contaminants such as water vapor (~10 vol%) and NO, and accelerated thermal aging (e.g., exposure to up to 850°C for several hours) to mimic lifetime degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: The porous high‐entropy oxide (HEO) overlayer, whose multi-element composition reduces surface free energy and provides a robust, defect‐rich interface.
generation.mechanism: The HEO overlayer lowers the driving force for metal nanoparticle sintering by reducing the overall surface free energy and creates a protective matrix that minimizes the adsorption of water and NO. Its intrinsic configurational disorder can also promote facile oxygen vacancy formation and exchange, enabling self‐regeneration of active sites during redox cycling. Together, these effects maintain small, highly active metal sites for oxidation while resisting common deactivation pathways.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the overcoated catalyst should exhibit a lower light‐off temperature (e.g., further decrease in T10 or T50 for CO/hydrocarbon oxidation), enhanced resistance to deactivation in the presence of H2O and NO, and significantly improved long‐term durability (e.g., minimal change in activity over hundreds of hours or during accelerated aging tests) without increasing the amount of platinum-group metals.
generation.baseline: The unmodified near‐equiatomic alloy catalyst, which shows good initial activity but degrades under transient low-temperature conditions and poisoning by water and NO, leading to increased oxidation temperatures and loss of activity over time.
generation.boundary: This intervention is predicted to be effective under typical automotive exhaust conditions and simulated accelerated aging regimes. Its benefits may diminish if the overcoat becomes too thick (limiting reactant accessibility) or if the operational conditions exceed the stability range of the HEO layer.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis is built by combining evidence of high‐entropy oxide-enabled sinter‐ and water‐resistance (e.g., as seen in PMC12224923::web::004 and PMC12224923::web::018) with insights into self‐regeneration driven by high entropy (PMC8505510::web::000), extended to the automotive catalyst regime. The new aspect here is the application of an ultrathin HEO overlayer as a singular, interface-engineering intervention, which has not yet been directly validated in this specific multi‐principal‐element automotive catalyst framework.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: one consisting of the unmodified near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy and the other with an ultrathin porous HEO overlayer applied under identical conditions. Subject both to simulated automotive exhaust testing featuring transient low temperatures (below 150 °C), controlled exposures to water vapor (~10 vol%) and NO, and accelerated aging cycles (e.g., aging at 850 °C for 2 hours followed by cyclic redox treatments). Compare light‐off curves (CO and hydrocarbon oxidation temperatures), poisoning tolerance, and activity retention over extended operational periods.
measurements: Temperature required for 10% and 50% conversion (T10 and T50) of CO and hydrocarbons.
Activity degradation rates during continuous operation and after accelerated aging cycles.
Microscopic analysis (e.g., HAADF-STEM) to assess nanoparticle sintering and overlayer structural integrity.
Surface composition (XPS) to verify resistance to water and NO adsorption.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEO-overcoated catalyst does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in lowering oxidation temperatures, resisting poisoning (i.e., comparable or faster deactivation under water/NO exposure), or maintaining nanoparticle size and activity over the accelerated aging tests relative to the unmodified catalyst, then the hypothesis is falsified.
